items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] I use AI to save time. So why am I working more?
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🔭 ✏️

This year, I’ve been building an AI social media production pipeline to promote the 25+ shows on the Autistic Culture Podcast Network. It took me a week of effort, but I managed to program Claude Code to talk to NotebookLM, which now feeds our YouTube, Instagram, and TikTok pipeline, and a task that used to take me a full day now runs in the background. The first time I ran a real batch through it, I felt the guilt of always being behind fade away. I could physically feel my nervous system recalibrating. Maybe for the first time since I was 10 years old, with these artificial intelligence agents, I could recapture the feeling of not being behind!

And then, the other shoe dropped. The next week, the automatic processing didn’t work. I had to rebuild the agent from scratch. Meanwhile, I was in the middle of building my next agent to send out press releases when new shows launch, but that got put on hold.  At about 3 a.m., I was in a full-on AI coding haze when I ran out of credits and had no choice but to go to bed. At that moment, I realized all this time I was trying to save by using AI was sure taking up a lot of time.

Business culture has one instrument for measuring AI, and it’s the stopwatch. Productivity!

Minutes saved. Output multiplied. Projects completed. Revenue up.

Every dashboard asks how much faster the company is moving. Are we working less, though? Because I, for one, have been working more and with a panic about not being left behind. Getting more done is not the same as making the work day less demanding.

The gap matters even more for neurodivergent founders like me. A report published in June by the U.K.’s Lilac Centre, based on a national survey of more than 600 neurodivergent entrepreneurs, found that 76% started their businesses specifically to work in a way that suited them, but 79% report workload-management or burnout challenges as a result.

The same report calls AI and digital tools “accessibility scaffolding,” and I’d back that up. I even wrote a book way back in 2023 about how AI could be used as an accessibility tool for neurodivergent people. I use AI daily to start tasks I’d otherwise stall on, to turn scattered thinking into a structured draft, to get past the executive-function wall that shows up when my monotropic flow is not flowing in the directions I need it to. I do not question that AI can take tasks off your plate. But, what I missed in my book, and I think others are missing, is the cost of using AI.

Call it the Automation Tax. It’s all the extra work you have to do to make the AI make your job go faster, and the expectation that now you can do things faster, you still need to use every working hour to get even more done. The speed got turned up, but the workload didn’t decrease.

Building the Autistic Culture Podcast Network pipeline taught me the size of that tax. Wiring three systems together, learning where each tool tends to fail so I know what to double-check; none of that showed up in an “hours saved per post” calculation.

Meanwhile, my workload never seemed to decrease. The hour saved was filled with the next task, because faster output means more time to plan and promote. Instead of writing my magnum opus or learning Italian with the time I saved, I found myself managing more agents. 

This is why when I use a tool now, I ask three questions. What exact task disappears? What new work shows up in its place? And do I really end up with fewer things to manage, or just different things?

 A single AI-drafted Instagram caption might save me only five minutes, but it removes the dread of staring at a blank box until the moment to post has passed; for a task that small, that’s an excellent return. Meanwhile, generating five newsletters in the time it used to take to write one still leaves five newsletters to fact-check, schedule, and defend if something in them is wrong. Output goes up, sure, but so does the workload.

If I can’t answer that last question: Do I really end up with fewer things to manage or different things, then the tool has just shifted or even increased the workload. 

The best AI tool isn’t the one that helps you produce the most. It’s the one that frees you up to do more of what you want to do.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] Thousands of security workers for Big Tech companies are on strike in California
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Security officers at some of the most prominent tech companies in Silicon Valley have been poised to walk off the job since voting to authorize a strike earlier this month. The workers have been in talks with major security contractors like Securitas and Allied Universal for months as they seek to reach a new contract agreement.

Now, as contract negotiations have stalled, 14,000 security officers represented by SEIU-United Service Workers West are striking across California. The union members took to the streets in San Francisco and Los Angeles at 4:30 a.m. local time on Friday to push for meaningful wage increases and better benefits. 

The SEIU-USWW campaign has highlighted the gulf between hourly pay for security workers and the deep coffers of the tech giants who use their services. While the workers are technically employed by third-party contractors, the union has said they provide building security for companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, Cisco, and Netflix; they also serve a variety of other employers, from hospitals to retailers. 

According to the union, some of the security contractors have proposed a mere $0.65 raise in hourly pay over the next two years; Allied Universal, the largest security firm in the world, reportedly offered a wage increase of just $0.25 per hour in 2027, with no raises for the following three years.

SEIU-USWW president David Huerta previously described this proposal as “shameful, wrong, and deeply, deeply disrespectful.” 

In a statement, an Allied Universal spokesperson said: “We have made substantial progress in negotiations as part of our commitment to finding common ground. We value the ongoing dialogue, have approached discussions with flexibility and a willingness to work collaboratively toward solutions, and remain focused on reaching a fair and mutually beneficial agreement.” (Securitas was not immediately available for comment.)

Security personnel have become even more critical as companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have faced threats amid mounting public distrust of AI. A few weeks ago, Business Insider reported that Anthropic had instructed its employees to work from home, in case their security officers decided to go on strike.

“Clearly, Anthropic understands how indispensable security workers are, even if the companies bargaining with them don’t,” Huerta told Bay Area public media outlet KQED recently. 

In the meantime, median pay for security workers in California remains around $20 per hour, according to an analysis by the UC Berkeley Labor Center. While median pay for security officers is higher in the Bay Area—closer to $24 per hour—that’s still significantly lower than the median wage for all workers in the region, which crosses $42 per hour.

In Los Angeles, median pay for security workers is less than $20 per hour, a figure noticeably lower than the median wage for all workers in the greater L.A. area, which is higher than $27 per hour.

According to the UC Berkeley analysis, more than 44% of all security officers in California qualify as low-wage workers; in the Bay Area, more than two-thirds of security workers are classified as low-wage. 

The SEIU-USWW members who went on strike Friday are aiming for hourly pay of $30, along with more affordable healthcare coverage, expanded retirement benefits, and robust training. Contract workers who provide ancillary services to tech companies have previously walked off the job, often ramping up public pressure on those employers to negotiate more favorable terms with third-party contractors. 

In its recent demonstrations, the union has pointed out that as the cost of living continues to rise precipitously in cities like San Francisco, security workers may eventually have no choice but to leave if their pay doesn’t improve—to the detriment of the many companies that have come to rely on their labor.

items.title: 🔓 [Fast Company] We know how to shape systems to better support working mothers. So why don’t we?
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🔭 ✏️

As more women join the workforce and gradually gain representation in leadership roles, the lack of resources like affordable childcare and paid maternity leave has become increasingly consequential. 

In the first half of last year, the U.S. saw the steepest decline of working mothers with children under 5 years old in 40 years, according to a University of Kansas study, and that decline has continued.

During this week’s Fast Company Innovation Festival, staff editor Shalene Gupta asked several mothers in senior leadership positions how we got here, what mothers need, and how we can improve workplaces and support systems accordingly.

We’ve been here before

Panelists noted that governments and workplaces have already shown that they can adapt.

Girls Who Code founder Reshma Saujani, now CEO of Moms First—an organization that advocates for paid leave and affordable childcare—said that during World War II, the Lanham Act created the country’s first national childcare program, supporting many of the millions of women who suddenly entered the workforce.

“The minute men came back to work, so what did we do? We dismantled all those childcare centers,” she said.

At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, women lost 1.5 million more jobs than men, according to Indeed’s Hiring Lab; even so, it was a time in which workplaces offered more flexibility for parents, and billions in government childcare funding helped more women enter or remain in the workforce. 

Then, those systems were shut down, too, Saujani said. 

Affordable childcare is a broadly popular concept

Families have made it clear that affordable childcare is a priority, she said, referencing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s emphasis on providing no-cost childcare. 

Another thing we learned during the pandemic, and are now seeing in response to AI, is “that companies can get really nimble, really quick” when growth and capital are on the line, said Alison Moore, CEO of Chief, a private membership network for women in leadership. 

Moore said we need to apply that same mindset to human capital—and the changes we’ve seen so far haven’t been enough.

Outside of the workplace, there are other gaps in available support for mothers, especially new mothers, said Latham Thomas, CEO and founder of the doula-training company Mama Glow and the nonprofit Mama Glow Foundation.

Doulas, for example, provide emotional and physical support and education, she said; but they also work to “ensure that there are systems in place when your baby arrives, so that when they leave, you can actually function.”

They look for gaps in care, Thomas said, and unfortunately, current systems in the U.S. often mean paying people to fill those gaps. The people in those caregiving professions aren’t well taken care of either, she said. 

“They’re underinsured, they’re under-resourced, they’re underpaid,” Thomas added. “And quite frankly, those are the people that we need to be shoring up the most support for financially, and building institutional frameworks for, to ensure that they can be a part of our journey as we advance as women.”

Saujani added that we already know what to do. “The question you’ve got to ask yourself is, why don’t we do it?”

The impossibility of being a working mother in America is due to intentional policy failures, Saujani said. “And every time we get close to fixing these structural failures, we get handed a culture war”—like the false choice between being a tradwife or a girlboss. 

Until we get past those divisions, she said, we can’t fix things to “finally build a country that works for mothers.”

🎨 🌾 🔧 🪶 🌲 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

More than 3 in 4 parents say relying on Boomer grandparents is essential to afford raising kids

Raising children is becoming more and more costly, and modern parents are feeling the strain. Now, according to one new report, grown adults with children are relying on their own parents in high numbers.

The data comes from a survey of 2,500 U.S. adults by the global market research company Ipsos for the 2026 BMO Real Financial Progress Index. The research found that the large majority of parents in the U.S. believe that the cost of raising children is “out of control,” with 82% agreeing with the sentiment. Meanwhile, even nonparents are concerned about the cost of raising children, as 79% wonder how their peers can afford to have families. 

“Raising kids has always been a labor of love, but right now, it is also a major feat of financial engineering with families torn between spending on the urgent and the important,” Robin Growley, U.S. Head of Consumer Products, BMO, said in a news release.

Growley continued, “Whether you are budgeting for diapers or dorm rooms, the absolute best antidote to daily financial stress is a clear, actionable plan.” 

For many modern parents, part of the plan seems to be relying on their own boomer parents to afford raising their kids. In 2026, 76% of parents with children under 18 say that receiving financial support from extended family is necessary to afford opportunities for their children. Likewise, 37% of parents expect financial help from their parents or grandparents over the next year and plan to ask for it. 

Mostly, that group is getting help with daily living expenses. 47% of those who will ask for help say they will receive cash for their everyday needs. 43% say the help will come in the form of free childcare, provided by grandparents, or help with the costs of childcare. 26% say their family is helping financially by putting away funds for the future for their children.

The need for financial assistance isn’t due to the fact that modern parents are lazy or wildly over-spending. Mainly, it has to do with how quickly the cost of raising children has gone up drastically in recent years. According to a 2026 Lending Tree analysis, since 2023, the annual cost of raising a young child has skyrocketed by nearly 36%, coming to about $30,000 per year, or $300,000 over 18 years. 

Interestingly, while financial help from family may go a long way, there’s an emotional tax that comes with it. Those who live close to aging parents and receive help with the costs of raising children are more likely financially overwhelmed than those who don’t (74% as opposed to 57%).  

Growley noted that the numbers likely reflect the sandwich generation’s attunement with the fact that their parents raising children also realize their aging parents will soon be relying on them, too. “Having a grandparent help raise your kids can be one of life’s greatest gifts, but family caregiving is often a reciprocal arrangement—and it can be a lot when you’re already stretched thin,” Growley said.
